memories.memory_text: I told Ted to stop staring at Christy—some things are out of our league, like filet mignon for hamburger guys. I could see him itching to say something dumb, so I hit him with the truth, juicy and raw.
I flipped open 'HEAVEN' and did my Ginger voice—'set it on VIBRATE, honey'—winking at Ted like I was handing him the keys to the kingdom. His face? Priceless.
I saw that look in Ted’s eyes—the dumb, dreamy kind—and I started yelling 'Danger, Will Robinson, danger' to stop him. He didn’t listen. He just walked away.
I hit Ted with the one-word joke—'MEATLOAF'—right after he puked in the sink, and the next thing I know he's staring at himself in the mirror like the word just cracked open the universe.
I was just standing there, probably looking at one of those dorky family photos, when Ted’s mom suddenly throws my name into the ring like I’m some kind of babysitter for his will-reading trip.

I remember leaning in close, my voice low but sharp—'Who the hell was your father?'—because one second we were joking about names, and the next this stunning driver was hugging Ted like he was grieving some dead legend.
I cranked up the rock music just to see Ted freak out—he told me not to touch anything, but come on, what’s a limo without a soundtrack?
I popped the Dom Perignon and got drenched in champagne—foam everywhere, right down my pants—and yeah, it was messy, but damn, did it feel like we’d stolen the good life for a minute.
I stuck my head out of the limo sunroof, wind blasting my face, and yelled, 'This is how the other half lives, bro—enjoy it while you can,' while Ted looked like he might puke or pass out.

I gawked so hard my jaw nearly hit the table when Zukerman said Ted owned the whole 'Heaven' empire—like, every magazine, theme park, and glittery piece of real estate. I couldn’t help but blurt out, 'Everything?' before anyone could shut me down.

When the screen lit up with Ted’s bio parents—especially his mom, practically spilling out of that gold top—I couldn’t resist cracking a joke under my breath about where Ted got his taste in girls, just loud enough for Billy to hear.
This place is my wet dream come true—women everywhere, topless, touching, and I don’t even care that Ted’s here ruining the vibe.
I couldn’t help shouting it—‘Oh baby, yes, yes, yes. Fuck me like you mean it’—while watching her rub lotion on her tits, and Ted had to elbow me back to reality.
I kicked open Ted's door waving the binoculars, yelling for him to come see something—couldn't wait, didn't care who he was talking to.
I flipped the lights off and shoved the binoculars into Ted’s hands, hissing for him to check it out—like I was handing him holy scripture instead of glass and plastic.
When he said we were dead and this was heaven, I didn’t laugh—instead, I ran with it, picturing a room made entirely of chocolate like it was the most obvious damn thing in the afterlife.
I yanked open the drawer and there they were—red silk panties, soft as sin. I held them up, inhaled that powdery scent, and said, 'Cha-ching. Jackpot.'

Ted snatched them from me, ripped them in half, and gave me that look—like I'd crossed a line. When the butler walked in, I just shrugged and said, 'A couple of boys fighting over a pair of red silk panties is nothing compared to what he's seen.'

I stood there watching Ted strut down the stairs with those twins on his arms, head high like he owned the place — and damn, he almost did. I couldn’t stop grinning; it was like watching a nerdy kid turn into a god right before my eyes.
I spun through the crowd, disco-ready, and shouted in his ear — 'A week ago you couldn’t get to second base, now you OWN second base!' — then we slapped hands like we’d won the damn Super Bowl.
I hopped out of that heavenly blue chopper right after Ted, planting a big kiss on the blonde pilot just so everyone could see—felt like we’d finally arrived, like we were untouchable.
Julie called me 'Don Corleone' and I shot back about Italian loafers—then offered to show her a hickey from Miss December, which totally grossed her out.
I called myself a 'very cunning linguist' and the next thing I knew, the flight attendant was yanking me toward the washroom like I’d just won a backstage pass.

I was handing my 'Heaven' flyer to Judy when her dad came storming in, knocking the whole stack out of my hands—next thing I know, they're floating down like some divine intervention, landing right at the feet of a group of hot girls who couldn't wait to grab them.
I saw Christy Malone turn around and say 'Hi, Teddy Bear' like it was nothing, and my whole body just locked up—cold, like I'd been slapped with a slab of frozen meat.
I called out 'Don't forget your broom!' after Ginger as she stormed off—couldn't help it, the witch gag was just too easy.
I leaned in and told Ted, 'Take your pick. They're IDENTICAL,' right after one of the Taylor Triplets gave him a look—he couldn't resist that.

I remember yelling that I loved those springy head puppies while Ted was on the phone ordering a mountain of junk, champagne in hand, the TV flashing gaudy gnomes like we were living in a fever dream.
I was already cranking the motor drive on my Nikon when Ted said 'Get them together,' and something just lit up in my chest—like, this was the moment, the real show was starting.

I held up the magazine and said, 'Holy stinkers, what were you thinking?'—then laughed because the whole hallway was already on fire and I wasn't about to let Ted's sad eyes stop me from throwing one more match.
I handed Julie the copy of 'Heaven' with a grin, telling her 'Page three' like it was the punchline to a joke only we were in on.

I saw her eyes get all watery reading the dedication, then the next second she's flipping to the pictorial and cracking up at Merkin in a wig—singing Barbra Streisand no less, with Molly practically draped over him.
I slapped on my best grin and hit Ted with that 'coxswain on the ship of life' line—classic Charlie—watched his face go from dead to slightly less dead.
When Ted and Julie started dancing to 'People,' I grabbed Jimmy and fake-sobbed, 'I'm a sucker for a happy ending,' then yelled 'Hold me' like it was the final act of a soap opera.
I was rolling around in that haystack, all three of the Taylor Triplets on me at once—laughing, pulling, biting—like a goddamn three-headed love monster.
I saw the triplets' kids peeking out from the haystack—many little versions of me—and I wasn't sure what to feel.

I watched Ted on that stupid talk show, all polished and grinning, talking about 'expanding beauty' while pinning some dumb rose to his jacket like he was doing something noble. 'The Girls of Xenia'? Jesus.

I cut through the crowd on the Harley, engine roaring, and stopped right in front of him—dress flapping, jacket zipped up. Said, 'Need a lift?' like it was no big deal, even though my heart was doing backflips.

I took the wheel and drove us out past Xenia, just me and Ted, heading down a dark country road with no destination he could guess. I told him it was the best hiding place in the world, and for once, I meant it without irony.
I remember the oak tree in the backyard—big enough to hide in, just like the rest of this oversized life I never asked for.
He didn’t build this place—he had it built, like it was just another transaction. I could hear the hollow pride in Ted’s voice, mistaking money for love.
He kept pushing me to expose Merk, like I owe him rebellion. But I told him—lemons into lemonade. I’m not chasing scandals just to prove I’m still sharp.

I watched Merkin in that ridiculous mustache, grinning like an idiot while crooning with a bunch of old people, and for a second, I couldn’t tell if we were the ones chasing justice or just a couple of assholes looking for a villain who didn’t exist.
I watched Merkin serve soup to that homeless guy, then gave Ted a look—like, 'See? This is what I meant.'
I called Ted and told him I had an anonymous tip with an address in Cincinnati—felt like crossing a line, but I said 'Let's do it' before he could ask questions.

I felt the heat of Ted leaning in, his voice dropping low like he was trying to hypnotize me with words, and for a second I almost believed him—until my eyes caught Merkin in full Barbra drag under the spotlight.
I was laughing in the rain with Ted, soaked and breathless, and for a second I let myself feel that stupid, giddy high—like any of it meant something.

I pulled away when he brought up that pictorial again—I had to say it straight: I hate 'The Girls of Xenia,' and the way he talks about it like it's just another job makes me wonder if he sees any of this as real.
I ran from Ted, water dripping down his face, calling after me—begging me to let him explain, like that would fix anything.
I unzipped my dress and let it drop, standing there naked in front of him—not because I wanted him to want me, but because I needed him to see how little it meant, how empty he really was.
I told him he didn’t know me at all, not even after seeing me naked—his magazine, his crush, all of it just noise, and I liked him better before he became this hollow version of himself.

Charlie stood there grinning, handing me a copy of 'Heaven'—some magazine he clearly thought mattered. I flipped to page three and saw it: 'To Julie, My Partner in Crime, With All the Love in the World.' My eyes stung before I could stop them.

I flipped ahead to check the 'Girls of Xenia' spread and froze—there was Principal Merkin in full drag, belting out a Barbra Streisand number. And in some shots, Molly was right there with him, like they were posing together. I muttered something about yellow journalism just to keep my voice steady.

I heard Ted say he was giving up the magazine to go to college, and when he joked about being a coxswain, I couldn’t help but say, ‘Very ambitious. I like that.’ It was the first time I believed he wasn’t just playing a role.
The song 'People' came on, and Ted held out his hand, saying it was our song. I took it and said, 'You better,' not knowing if I meant the dance or something more—but for once, I didn’t pull away.

I stood on the deck of the sailboat, the wind sharp against my face, watching the sun bleed gold into the Pacific while Ted steered us into the glare—like some punchline to a romance we never actually wrote.

memories.memory_text: I was in the middle of a dramatic exit when this guy knocked into me, and then he just blurts out that my biological parents died in the Amazon from piranhas—like it was nothing.
I remember saying, 'They didn't want me when I was born. Why should I care... if they're dead,' and feeling the weight of it hang in the air, candles flickering like the silence after.
I snapped at Charlie, 'Oh, how inappropriate is that!' when he started pawing through my mother's lingerie like it was some sick trophy case.
After we ripped the panties apart fighting over them, the butler walked in and we both stood there like guilty idiots, hiding the pieces behind our backs.
I saw the price tag on the sleeve and couldn't believe the number—my whole life I'd never seen that many zeros on a receipt.
Ginger whispered in my ear about money only mattering to those who don't have it—I felt her breath, the smoothness of her voice, like it was supposed to mean something bigger than just clothes.

I stood up in front of all those reporters, lights blazing, and said I’d been editor of the high school paper in Xenia, Ohio—won awards, made a difference. Felt proud saying it out loud, like I finally had permission to matter.
I joked about having my dad’s taste in women and cars—faster, the better—and winked. The room chuckled, Billy gave me a thumbs-up, and for a second, it felt like we were in on the same joke.
I told Merkin that turning down the magazine would be insane—this was my dream, the kind every guy would kill for.
I reminded him about the Rolex I sent, and watching him reluctantly hand it back—I could tell it killed him to do it.
I remember hearing Uncle Billy call me the 'Titan of Tushies' and laughing—really laughing—because for once, someone important was praising me like I mattered, like I was built for something big.
My dad stood in the doorway with that chore list again, and I just nodded and turned back to the screen—couldn't let him interrupt the moment, even if I saw how he hesitated before leaving.
I stood on the ottoman while the tailor fitted me, looking down at them as they begged me to give up the magazine—like I was supposed to trade everything I built just to fit their little dream.
I told them I was never meant to be raised by grocers—and when I stormed off, I knocked over the family photo, the glass shattering like something final, though I didn’t mean to break it.

I had all four penthouse suites booked under my name, Dom Perignon in hand, ordering a hundred and seventeen of those ugly gnomes and ten dozen springy-head puppies—this was my show, and I wasn’t just crashing the prom, I was rewriting it.

Merkin showed up like some buzzkill prophet, talking about laws and developing minds—like we weren’t all just kids trying to feel alive for one night—and when he said he called the cops, I swear the whole floor dropped, but I made sure he saw the look before I ran.

I was just walking out with the crowd after prom, still buzzing from the night, when Julie came out of nowhere on that Harley—purple dress, leather jacket, completely unexpected. She looked back and said, 'Need a lift?'—and before I could overthink it, I was on the bike, holding onto her, wind rushing as we sped off.
I asked Julie if my real father would’ve just bought me a stadium instead of teaching me how to play ball—like her dad phoned in the treehouse, maybe mine would’ve done the same.
I told Julie that even when she infuriates me, I still want to kiss her. She said I never do.
I hung up the phone after Julie told me the target was on the move—Cincinnati, some anonymous tip—and all I said was, 'Let's do it.'

I was soaked and laughing with Julie in the rain after finding the perfect centerfold, but then she turned serious and said she despised 'The Girls of Xenia'—my own project—and I had to tell her it was about keeping a promise, not arousal.

I remember unzipping Christy’s top, my hands slow on the zipper, catching that first glimpse of her bare back—smooth, long, and glowing under the strobe lights. She didn’t say a word, just gave me that coy look over her shoulder, like she’d been waiting for this exact moment.

I remember her from second grade—blue gingham dress, pulling her ponytail. Now she's here in the shower, unzipping her top, taking off her clothes. I'm outside the shower, squirming in my clothes, camera in hand, not sure what comes next.

I was still dripping from the shower when I chased Julie down the hall, yelling for her to wait—just let me explain—but she bolted into the girls’ restroom like I was the last person she ever wanted to see. I stood there, alone in the quiet, then stepped inside after her.
I saw Julie undress right in front of me, standing there naked by the sinks, and I couldn’t look away—not because of her body, but because I actually cared about her.

Her dress was back on before I could say anything, and then my phone rang—Uncle Billy screaming about the magazine, while she just walked away, like I’d already become one of the fake things she hated.
I sat there in the conference room and heard Uncle Billy call me 'the kid' like I wasn't even a real part of the team, like none of my ideas had ever mattered.
I realized right then that Billy was letting me take the fall for the magazine issue, shifting all the blame onto me even though I thought we were on the same page.

I was sitting at my father's desk, buried in reports and charts, when the sound of girls laughing by the pool pulled me to the window—watching them, I felt hollow, not happy, and I realized the life I built wasn't what I thought it would be.
I remember seeing those baby photos in the scrapbook—me through a nursery window, like they were watching from a distance, never stepping in. I never knew they’d been keeping track all along.

I stood there holding the weight of that empire they built for me, and all I could think was: my real parents are in Xenia, I’ve hurt them, and the girl I love would never look at me the same if I took this.
I stood up from the couch, my eyes wet, and told them everything I am is because of you—then asked if they could ever forgive me, staring at the restored portrait above the mantle.
After Mom scolded me for saying 'shit,' I told them I'm really in deep shit and need their help—knowing I couldn't fix this alone, despite how much I hate admitting it.

I burst into the stockholders' meeting holding up a can of peaches, my dad right behind me, and shouted over Uncle Billy—suddenly every eye was on me, confused, waiting to see if I’d choke. I could feel my hands shaking, but I made myself walk to the podium and say what needed to be said about canned peaches and keeping promises.

After the applause, I turned to Uncle Billy and told him family is about love, not blood—then fired him, watching the grin drop off his face as he begged for mercy. I didn’t flinch, even when he called me 'Ted-baby' and reminded me he was my uncle.

I watched the final layouts, listened to the team, and felt this quiet certainty—like I wasn’t just playing a role anymore. When they said the magazine was going to press, it didn’t feel like luck. It felt like I’d earned it.

Someone handed me Julie’s article, and I read the last line out loud—'remember, always, where he came from.' I don’t know if I believed I deserved those words, but for once, I didn’t make a joke. I just stood there, quiet.
I told Julie I was giving up the magazine, going to college, and wanted her as my first mate—she smiled, and for the first time, I meant it when I said I wanted to be a coxswain.
I asked Julie to dance when 'People' came on—she took my hand, we kissed, and I felt like everything I ever wanted wasn't money or power, but just this.
I remember the sun bleeding gold and red into the Pacific as we cut through the waves—Julie at the helm, me beside her, not saying much, just letting the silence say it all.
